Ramaphosa- The Economy

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The nine years of the Jacob Zuma era have been plagued with economic uncertainty and now that it’s the end of an era. Can Ramaphosa carry the ailing South African economy to a prosperous future?

Unique Selling Point:
Corruption, state capture, struggling SOEs and economic downgrades are words that colour the Jacob Zuma presidential legacy. With Parliament electing Cyril Ramaphosa as state president and the country oozing with optimism, will the South African economy reclaim the stability it has missed in the past nine years?

Summary:
Certainly a friend to business South Africa, Cyril Ramaphosa’s election as President of the ANC brought a positive response to the Rand. Following former president Jacob Zuma’s resignation from the state office and Ramaphosa being elected and sworn in by parliament, the new leader inherits a lot of ill governance. Debt ridden state owned enterprises are in shambles to say the least.

Eskom, SAA, PRASA are some of the SOEs that were collapsed by state capture under Jacob Zuma. More than once the country was downgraded by Ratings Agencies relegating South Africa to junk status and loss of investor confidence. Most importantly free education and the National Health Insurance were introduced without a clear plan of where their funding will come from. These are some of the issues Ramaphosa will inherit from the Zuma presidency and with unemployment at 26.7 percent, the new president has a lot of remedying to do to regain economic confidence.

As welcome as the change in leadership is, it certainly has an insurmountable task ahead, but is Cyril Ramaphosa a guarantee to a brighter economic future for South Africa. Carte Blanche finds out.

Press Release:


Corruption, State capture, struggling SOEs and economic downgrades are words that colour the Jacob Zuma presidential legacy. With Parliament electing Cyril Ramaphosa as State president and the country oozing with optimism, will the South African economy reclaim the stability it has missed in the past nine years?

Script:


Zuma: Thank you...We'll meet somewhere

LInk: Over the last 9 years South Africa was plagued with economic instability under the Jacob Zuma regime. What will it take take for the new Ramaphosa administration to bring positive change and prosperity for all.

Parliament visual everyone standing ovation... into song...
Sound up... Start with song …. Rise up Ramaphosa, the time is here... unity...

Lesiba: The country is elated with the election of Cyril Ramaphosa and concluded that the economy is as a result over this one outcome is better.

Rudie: I think that definitely South Africans can be optimistic and that we can move forward with this.

Chris Yelland: He brings to the table a new view on the energy sector in South Africa, on state owned enterprises, on the economy of South Africa.

Link: The general euphoria amongst South Africans is that there's finally hope for a stable economy, but what does that actually mean for the average person on the street?

Irvin Jim: Poverty is written in the faces of our people

VO: General Secretary of Numsa, Irvin Jim is not that optimistic, especially when it comes to the issue of unemployment.

Irvin Jim: They say unemployment is about 27,7% and from where we're sitting unemployment is about 36%, If you are looking at the people who don't have a plate of food is about 30.4M south Africans who don't have a plate of food. We're sitting on a ticking bomb. They are going to do everything around Cyril to create the impression that they will find solutions, but there is no revolutionary agenda that the ANC is Driving. So the working class is in a crisis.

VO: However, sentiment is a big driver for markets and already the rand is at it's strongest since 2015. Economist Lesiba Mothata says that with investor confidence somewhat restored, the economy should stabilise and the ordinary man in the street will ultimately benefit.

Lesiba: If you get confidence right so that you get the man on the street believing that when they go to the shop they will find the price what they're paying on maize or what whatever, is going to go lower going forward it induces confidence, so the South African reserve bank says under their condition, when a consumer is feeling this way and you have the business people also feeling this way, you can eek out between 0.4 and 1 percentage points of growth.

VO: With the introduction of a national minimum wage of R20,00 per hour, the hope is that this will begin to address the issues of inequality. South Africa is still one of the most unequal societies in the world.

Cyril in Sona sound up: This year we will introduce the first minimum wage our country has ever had.

IrvinJim: Cyril Ramaphosa as the leader of business government has been the one who is basically at the centre of the current colonial wage, in terms of the national minimum wage where workers are to be paid R20/h. We reject that and we saying that the working class must basically continue to demand a national minimum wage which must be a living wage

VO: But can South Africa's economy accommodate a living wage, at a time when State owned enterprises have drained the country's resources incurring a cumulative debt of astronomic proportions.
Denel has outstanding debt to the tune of R678m
Transnet sits at R124,7 billion rand in the red
PetroSA made a net loss of R1.4bn
SAA has an outstanding debt of R13.8 billion and rising
And Eskom released its results last month, revealing a R367 billion debt

Link: The magnitude of Eskom's debt has the potential to plunge the country into darkness and to lead us to financial ruin

VO: Energy Analyst Chris Yelland says, that Eskom needs immediate intervention and he’s drawn up a 50 point plan on how the enterprise can be rescued.

Chris: Well the situation is dire, they've just had a 5Billion rand bridging finance from the PIC but they need 20 Billion this month and that doesn't solve Eskom's problems in the months ahead. Eskom's default can trigger the need for government to step in in terms of it's government guarantees, this could affect the national sovereign credit rating and put massive strain on the economy.

Claire: So is recapitalisation the solution?

Chris: You cannot just pour money into a deep hole, you have to address the core issues of Eskom and in my view that means a fundamental restructuring of the electricity supply industry in SA, from generation, transmission and distribution, including municipal distribution.

Claire: What role does President Ramaphosa have in the restructuring of Eskom?

Chris: Cyril Ramaphosa has played a key role in the electricity, in the energy and the Eskom sector in the past and I think he needs to be involved in the future.

VO: Burdensome and mismanaged State Owned Enterprises need urgent restructuring and SAA should be one of the first on the list, says Rudie Heyneke from OUTA .

Rudie: I Think that SAA was captured in another way. If you at the role of the board and the role of the execs, they not supposed to cross over, and it happened the board came in and interfered with the operations of SAA.

Cyril: We will also remove board members from any role of procurement.

VO: In his state of the Nation Address President Ramaphosa did not mince his words regarding the fate of SOES.

Rudie: I think the first thing that the president should do, is to take SAA away from treasury and put it into a department like the department of Transport
where it is supposed to be. Use the minister that's there to keep an eye on the board and keep the board and the execs accountable.

Claire: What could turn SAA around?

Rudie: I think the government must really look again at Privatisation of the national carrier, with a agreement that this PPP will still carry the national flag. It is a concept that worked very well at Telkom, and I think that it can work on more SOES.

VO: The president was hard hitting over the issue of an over abundance of State departments, which are also putting pressure on the fiscus due to their infrastructure needs.

Rudie: At this stage we have more than 30 government departments, in the previous administrations we had just over 20. You know you look at government buildings, for every new department, there's ministers that were appointed, deputy ministers, Dgs, public servants and it's a huge expenditure.

Link: With an already strained economy and empty coffers, one has to wonder, where will the money come from to fund free education and the looming prospect of National Health Insurance.

Lesiba: Free tertiary education it's a legitimate concern, it's going to arrive from taxes. Already the national treasury was clear that, they are likely to introduce 14% VAT on petrol, online transactions, also don't pay VAT, they are likely to introduce that, we might be paying luxury goods taxes and NHI it's still a debate and it's not implemented because its funding model is not clear at this point in time.

VO: It's true that a new era has dawned but the hard work still needs to be done, and the ratings agencies Standard and Poors and Fitch may not be that quick to ride the wave of optimism

Claire: How will ratings agencies view us?

Lesiba: There is a rule of thumb. If your debt level are around 60% of GDP, you require growth rate in a sustainable level of about 4%, that way it stops the further downgrade and it might be considered for further upgrades going forward.

VO: Moody's Investors Service who had held out on a downgrade in November last year, will deliver it's assessment in March, and President Ramaphosa is targeting a GDP growth of 3% to get the country’s economy to a competitive level, but is this possible?

Lesiba: Can you believe that the economic growth in this country resides in four cities. Cape Town, Johannesburg, durban and Pretoria, if the new administration comes in and considers to diversify the economy away from the four cities because it's when you do that, that you will be able to build a new economy along side the existing one, and doing it you actually can double the outcomes of what you now have.

Link: President Cyril Ramaphosa is under pressure to show change is coming, and the first real indicator of his resolve will be on Wednesday when the budget is presented.

Claire: Can one man really bring about the economic miracle that everyone is hoping for?

Lesiba: He needs to prove that, whether it's a new dawn or a lame duck situation. If it's a new dawn for whom much is given, much is required. And that requirement goes beyond dealing with corruption and unshackling this economy. But a Lame duck situation is where we continue on the status quo.

Cyril: Fellow South Africans, now is the time for change

FIN

More than once the country was downgraded by Ratings Agencies relegating South Africa to junk status and loss of investor confidence. Most importantly free education and the National Health Insurance were introduced without a clear plan of where their funding will come from. These are some of the issues Ramaphosa will inherit from the Zuma presidency and with unemployment at 26.7 percent, the new president has a lot of remedying to do to regain economic confidence. As welcome as the change in leadership is, it certainly has an insurmountable task ahead, but is Cyril Ramaphosa a guarantee to a brighter economic future for South Africa. Carte Blanche finds out.
